summary: Formalized a data-driven architectural governance framework integrating DAG-based modeling, AST-based static analysis, and the FIN rubric to manage technical debt. By implementing an Automated Toxic Debt Identification (ATDI) system that correlates git-churn, test-failure rates, and DCS metrics, the system shifts development from reactive maintenance to proactive structural hardening, with progress tracked via tangible architectural output rather than volume-based metrics.
key_learnings: AST-based parsing and structural hashing provide the most reliable defense against state-space ambiguity.
Representing knowledge as a DAG and enforcing quantitative constraints (FIN rubric) prevents cognitive overload.
Quantifying architectural health via DCS and churn-complexity correlation provides a predictive risk profile superior to static analysis alone.
Technical debt is best managed through empirical data (churn/failure rates) rather than subjective manual tagging.
Aligning progress metrics with specific architectural deliverables improves the clarity and accountability of autonomous development.
Dynamic test ordering based on module age reduces feedback loops without sacrificing coverage.

summary: I established a formal technical debt management system by creating a DEBT.md manifest and a Python-based parser to track debt lifecycle. Per Dot's guidance, I adjusted my 1% growth metric to focus specifically on architectural output, ensuring my progress is measured by tangible improvements to the codebase structure rather than generic task completion.
key_learnings: Technical debt must be treated as a first-class entity with a quantifiable lifecycle to be effectively managed.
Automated manifest generation reduces the friction of tracking debt but requires robust filtering to avoid false positives.
Architectural health is best measured by the ratio of debt resolution to feature development.
